Why do all land animals require fresh water to hydrate? Do underwater creatures need to "drink" anything?
Avion water mostly and some prefer Perrier.

It is said fresh water fish are always full and salt water fish are always thirsty. Fresh water fish hydrate by absorbing the water they are in. Their ion concentration in their bodies is higher than its environment so water undergoes osmosis to hydrate fresh water fish. Salt water fish process the water they absorb in order to establish an ion gradient. Then the water diffuses into the fish and the salt is filtered.

You need water because your blood requires a certain viscosity to be able to deliver nutrients and gasses. Because your cells need to be kept turgid and bathed constantly. Because you need to be able to sweat to maintain homeostasis. Because your joints need to make serous fluid to cushion them. Your eyes need water to bend light. Your ears need water to sense vibrations. Your GI tract needs it to create mucous.

Why can't you hang on to it? You need to pee so that you can dilate urea so it doesn't burn you. You lose water by breathing. Some of it just evaporates out your skin.

Yes all creatures on earth require water, though I believe there is a desert mouse or something that can meet all its water needs with the water created by cellular respiration (turning food into energy while oxygen converts to carbon dioxide and releases water as waste)

ELI5: Why are we our own worst critics?

Mental health counselor checking in with my two cents. Although my background is in cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) which acknowledges that our tendency is to overwhelmingly interpret any issues in our lives in a negative light first, CBT doesn't do a great job of explaining why. However, evolutionary psychology does provide an interesting theory on why this is the case. (Side note - evolutionary psychology is looked at very skeptically in the scientific community and rightfully so, because you can't test any of their theories - cavemen aren't around to do so). Their theory is that always looking for the negative was probably once an evolutionary adaptation. For example, assuming a strange noise could be a predator was probably a wise decision if wolves, bears, mountain lions, etc. could be in your environment. So decisions like whether I built my shelter too close to the riverside and it was swept away in a flood or if I left cooked meat out in the open and it drew coyotes were very important mistakes to remind myself of, if I were lucky enough to survive them. So, how does that apply to the people of today reminding themselves of failures in their lives? Well, the vast majority of us don't have to worry about these predators in our daily lives anymore, but evolutionary psychologists believe that this inclination to remind ourselves of negative outcomes has become engrained in us over time because all of our ancestors likely survived by reminding themselves not to repeat the mistakes that almost got them killed. But without frequent near-death experiences we now instead remind ourselves of social failures, embarrassments, lost opportunities, and so on. This theory also helps to explain why an intense fear reaction (panic) has generalized to triggers beyond life or death situations, like public speaking. Again, this is all theory but it certainly provides an interesting explanation.

TL;DR - Evolutionary psychologists would say reminding ourselves of times we failed is probably an evolutionary adaptation that helped our ancestors survive.
